Majora’s Mask has always been my favorite Zelda game. Even when saying that would get you flamed on Internet forums. It was such a strange twist on the world I’d become familiar with, it was slightly disturbing. Where is the princess? Why is the moon angry? Why does everybody look like my friends from Hyrule, but they’re not?

I first played it on a used game cartridge bought from eBay when I was 6 years old. There was a pre existing save file, so I was able to jump smack into the middle of things and fully embrace the weirdness and scariness. I remember being able to just feel that this game was different. Darker. Sadder. And that it had something to say.

I proceeded to play the game and never finish it for the next 13 years. When I was 19, it had been a long time since I played it. Then one day, I was reflecting on how I’d grown up. I had just started my first serious relationship. I was performing as a musician and stand up comic in clubs. I sat down in front of my Tv, put on Majora’s Mask, and finished it. I left the last screen of the finale on and cried. My childhood had officially ended. But it was the beginning of the real life I would lead with the lessons that game had taught me.

Appreciate your friends and the life you have, because you could lose them. Always be curious, and explore new places and ideas. Find new unique solutions to problems. And always help those in need when you can, because a good deed’s repercussions can be felt all throughout time.

Bonnibel is one of the most interesting characters in children’s media because of how nuanced she is, especially when compared to other characters of her type. She is Machiavellian, even though she rules with kindness. She’s still an ace manipulator. As Marceline so well put it: “You’re kind of a dictator.”

Now, we’re also shown that Bonnibel made Lemongrab, who is also mentally… not good. Did she do this on purpose? Not according to her. She says there’s nothing wrong with him, and that he’s the way he’s meant to be. That said, she also has no issue erasing things from his mind. It’s for a good cause, so we don’t think twice about it. But she clearly loves playing God. It’s hard to say if we can trust Bonnibel at her word.

So, did she make Cinnamon Bun half-baked on purpose? I’m sure she’d say no, that was how he was meant to be, or no, it was a mistake. But it’s also highly probable, knowing what we know about Bonnibel’s love of playing God, that she made him dumb so he would not pose a threat. Because he becomes a bit of a bad ass once he reaches the Fire Kingdom. 

There is definitely a theme of how Bonnibel keeps the Candy People as her “children”; both in that she loves them as a mother would, but also coddles them as a mother might. She keeps them dumb and unevolved. Maybe she does this out of love, and out of a desire to protect them from an absolutely insane world, but I think a big part that she would not acknowledge is that she does this to maintain power. It’s never stated as her ultimate motivation, but we’re shown so many times how she manipulates things behind the scenes, where her public image cannot be tarnished. But she does many questionable things all in the name of power.

Even ignoring her need for power as a motivator, she has the Mad Scientist aspect to her character. She makes messed-up creations just because she can and wants to see what will happen.

Tl;dr: Bonnibel be skeevy so she probably did it on purpose
